rules.quote: This is done with the clocking element, whose value is a nonempty list of dictionaries. Each dictionary (called a *clocking item*) defines a clock and reset signal. The clock signal is the field called clock. The reset signal is the field called reset.
rules.statement: Each peripheral must specify clocking via a nonempty list of clocking items, each defining clock and reset in fields named clock and reset.

rules.quote: If there are several, exactly one of the items' dictionaries should also have a boolean field called primary set to true.
rules.condition: When there are several clocking items
rules.statement: Exactly one clocking item dictionary should have boolean field primary set to true.

rules.quote: This primary clock used to clock any device interfaces, indicating to the top level if asynchronous handling of the bus interface is needed.
rules.statement: The primary clock is used to clock any device interfaces.

rules.quote: Resets within the design are asynchronous active low (see below). Resets within the design are asynchronous active low, where the assertion of the reset is asynchronous to any clock, but deassertion is synchronized to the clock of the associated storage element.
rules.statement: Resets within the design are asynchronous active low: assertion is asynchronous to any clock, deassertion is synchronized to the clock of the associated storage element.

rules.quote: Special care will be required for security sensitive storage elements. Security storage elements might "leak" sensitive state content, and should be handled with care regardless of reset methodology. By "care" an example would be to reset their value synchronously at a time after chip-wide reset, to a value that is randomized so that the Hamming distance between the register value and all zeros cannot produce information available to an attacker.
rules.statement: Security sensitive storage elements need special care, e.g. synchronous reset after chip-wide reset to a randomized value.

rules.quote: To allow these blocks to be described, the clock and reset fields of an item are optional.
rules.condition: For blocks that generate clocks or resets
rules.statement: The clock and reset fields of a clocking item are optional.

rules.quote: However, the primary clock must have both.
rules.statement: The primary clock item must have both clock and reset fields.

rules.section_title: Details and rationale for asynchronous active low reset strategy
rules.quote: Asynchronous active low incurs slightly more area and requires more hand-holding, but is more common. Synchronous active high is slightly more efficient, but requires the existence of a clock edge to take effect.
rules.statement: Tradeoff notes on asynchronous active low versus synchronous active high reset are informative only.

rules.quote: Peripherals can connect to the chip bus.
rules.statement: Peripherals can connect to the chip bus.

rules.quote: All peripherals are assumed to have registers, and are thus required to expose at least one device interface on the chip bus.
rules.statement: Every peripheral must expose at least one device interface on the chip bus.

rules.quote: Peripherals can act as a bus host on some occasions, though for full chip simplicity the preferred model is for the processor to be primary host.
rules.statement: Peripherals can act as bus host on some occasions, though the processor being primary host is preferred.

rules.quote: The bus_interfaces attribute in the configuration file should contain a list of dictionaries, describing the interfaces that the peripheral exposes.
rules.statement: The bus_interfaces attribute should contain a list of dictionaries describing the interfaces the peripheral exposes.

rules.quote: All peripherals use TileLink-UL (TileLink-Uncached-Lite, aka TL-UL) as their interface to the framework. To signify this, the peripheral must have a protocol of tlul.
rules.statement: The peripheral must have protocol of tlul since all peripherals use TL-UL.

rules.quote: Each entry must also contain a direction. This must either be host or device.
rules.statement: Each bus interface entry must contain a direction of either host or device.

rules.quote: All bus hosts must use the same clock as the defined primary host clock.
rules.statement: All bus hosts must use the same clock as the defined primary host clock.

rules.quote: An entry may also include a name. This name is added as a prefix to the module's top-level port names.
rules.statement: An entry may include a name, which is added as a prefix to the module's top-level port names.

rules.quote: This is optional unless there is another entry in the list with the same direction (in which case, the port names would collide).
rules.condition: When another entry in the list has the same direction
rules.statement: The name field must be provided to avoid port name collisions.

rules.quote: Each item of the form name in the interrupt list expects a module output named intr_name_o.
rules.condition: For each name in the interrupt list
rules.statement: The module must have an output named intr_name_o for each interrupt name.

rules.quote: All lowRISC peripheral designs must conform to this register specification.
rules.statement: All lowRISC peripheral designs must conform to the register specification.

rules.quote: Where possible (exceptions for inherited IP that is too tricky to convert) all interrupts shall have common naming, hardware interfaces, and software interfaces.
rules.statement: All interrupts shall have common naming, hardware interfaces, and software interfaces.

rules.quote: Currently, all wired CIP interrupts in OpenTitan use active-high level-triggering.
rules.statement: Wired CIP interrupts use active-high level-triggering.

rules.quote: See the example file above for one possible use of this schema. Key: name; Kind: required; Type: string; Description of Value: Name of the interrupt
rules.statement: Each interrupt_list entry must have a required name key of type string.

rules.quote: Key: desc; Kind: optional; Type: string; Description of Value: Description of the interrupt
rules.statement: Each interrupt_list entry may have an optional desc string.

rules.quote: Key: type; Kind: optional; Type: string; Description of Value: Select between "Event" and "Status" types, default is "Event" if unspecified.
rules.statement: Each entry may have an optional type, Event or Status, defaulting to Event if unspecified.

rules.quote: A peripheral generates a separate wired interrupt for each interrupt source, which are all routed to the target's interrupt controller.
rules.statement: A peripheral generates a separate wired interrupt for each interrupt source.

rules.quote: This is distinct from another possible model in which each peripheral would send only one interrupt, and the processor would disambiguate by querying the peripheral to figure out which interrupt was triggered.
rules.statement: Peripherals do not send a single combined interrupt for the processor to disambiguate by querying the peripheral.

rules.quote: By default for every peripheral, three registers are automatically created to manage the interrupts (as defined in the 'interrupt_list' of the .hjson file). These registers are named INTR_STATE, INTR_ENABLE and INTR_TEST, and are placed in that order automatically by the reggen tool at the top of the peripheral's address map. There is one bitfield in each register per interrupt.
rules.statement: INTR_STATE, INTR_ENABLE and INTR_TEST registers are created at the top of the address map in that order, one bitfield per interrupt.

rules.quote: (It is currently an error if the .hjson defines more than 32 interrupts for each peripheral.) The function of each register is explained in the following table.
rules.statement: The .hjson must not define more than 32 interrupts per peripheral.

rules.quote: Name: INTR_STATE; Offset: 0x0; Desc: holds the current state of the interrupt (may be RO or W1C depending on "IntrT"). Name: INTR_ENABLE; Offset: 0x4; Desc: enables/masks the output of INTR_STATE to create the wired interrupt signal intr_o. Name: INTR_TEST; Offset: 0x8; Desc: write-only (wo) register which asserts the interrupt for testing purposes.
rules.statement: INTR_STATE at offset 0x0 holds interrupt state, INTR_ENABLE at 0x4 masks it to intr_o, INTR_TEST at 0x8 is write-only and asserts the interrupt.

rules.quote: The contents of the INTR_STATE register are not qualified by INTR_ENABLE, but rather show the raw state of all latched hardware interrupt events.
rules.statement: INTR_STATE shows raw latched interrupt events and is not qualified by INTR_ENABLE.

rules.quote: When creating an interrupt in a peripheral, we can identify two distinct behaviors a designer may choose to implement.
rules.statement: A designer may choose between Event and Status interrupt behaviors.

rules.quote: The current interrupt can only be cleared by an acknowledgement from the handler (ack is a W1C operation to INTR_STATE in this mode). The event is cleared/acknowledged by a sw write of this bitfield, as INTR_STATE has W1C behaviour in this mode.
rules.statement: The interrupt is cleared only by a software W1C write of the INTR_STATE bitfield.

rules.quote: Status type: So long as the input is persistently true, trigger interrupt requests, including immediately after the previous request has been acknowledged.
rules.condition: Status type interrupt, input persistently true
rules.statement: Interrupt requests are triggered while input is true, including immediately after the previous request is acknowledged.

rules.quote: A persistent *Status* might be any conditional expression evaluating truthfully, such as a counter value currently exceeds a threshold, or the system being in a particular abstract state, such as an error state it cannot recover from on its own. Choosing to generate interrupts based on instantaneous events or persistent status signals can make it easier to write SW handlers that are simple and race-free.
rules.statement: Designers may generate interrupts from instantaneous events or persistent status, making software handlers simpler and race-free.

rules.quote: Using level-triggered wired interrupts, this is signaled by latching intr_o high (request) when the event occurs, and resetting intr_o low (ack) when software has finished executing its handler. The event is latched into the corresponding bitfield of INTR_STATE when it occurs.
rules.statement: When the event occurs it is latched into the INTR_STATE bitfield and intr_o is latched high until acknowledged, then low.

rules.quote: The generic component prim_intr_hw can generate the correct hardware when parameterized with .IntrT("Event").
rules.statement: prim_intr_hw parameterized with .IntrT("Event") can generate Event interrupt hardware.

rules.quote: Status type interrupts create a wired level-triggered interrupt signal directly from the input signal from hardware (only qualified by INTR_ENABLE). If the input signal is asserted, then the wired interrupt is constantly asserted, effectively issuing interrupt requests continuously.
rules.statement: A status type interrupt must drive a wired level-triggered interrupt directly from the hardware input signal, qualified only by INTR_ENABLE, staying asserted while the input is asserted.

rules.quote: With this interrupt type, the acknowledgement part of the req/ack handshake is an intervention from sw which causes the input signal from hardware to return to an inactive state. This means that the wired interrupt does not deassert until the root cause of the hardware input signal is addressed.
rules.statement: The wired status interrupt must not deassert until the root cause of the hardware input signal is addressed by software intervention.

rules.quote: Software cannot acknowledge this interrupt request using the INTR_STATE register, which has (ro) access permissions in this context.
rules.statement: Software cannot acknowledge a status type interrupt through INTR_STATE, which is read-only (ro) in this context.

rules.quote: The generic component prim_intr_hw can generate the correct hardware when parameterized with .IntrT("Status").
rules.statement: The generic component prim_intr_hw can generate the correct status interrupt hardware when parameterized with .IntrT("Status").

rules.quote: If SW cannot address the root cause of the interrupt, or wishes to defer handling, it should mask the interrupt, either at the peripheral or at some point further up the tree such as at the PLIC.
rules.condition: SW cannot address the root cause or wishes to defer handling
rules.statement: Software should mask the interrupt, at the peripheral or further up the tree such as the PLIC.

rules.quote: Masking at the peripheral can be achieved by clearing the corresponding bit in INTR_ENABLE.
rules.statement: Masking at the peripheral can be achieved by clearing the corresponding bit in INTR_ENABLE.

rules.quote: Taking an interrupt foo as an example, the block diagram below shows one possible hardware implementation.
rules.statement: The block diagram shows one possible hardware implementation of interrupt foo; other implementations are permitted.

rules.quote: Within the register file, the event triggers the setting of the associated bit in the INTR_STATE register to 1.
rules.statement: The event must set the associated bit in INTR_STATE to 1.

rules.quote: Additionally, a write of 1 of the associated foo bit of the INTR_TEST register can set the corresponding INTR_STATE bit.
rules.condition: Write of 1 to the foo bit of INTR_TEST
rules.statement: A write of 1 to the associated foo bit of INTR_TEST can set the corresponding INTR_STATE bit.

rules.quote: The output of the INTR_STATE register becomes the outgoing interrupt to the processor after masking (ANDing) with the value of INTR_ENABLE.
rules.statement: The outgoing interrupt intr_foo_o must be the INTR_STATE output ANDed with INTR_ENABLE.

rules.quote: Note that the handling of the ro/rw1c functionality of the INTR_STATE register allows software to control the clearing of the INTR_STATE content. A write of 1 to the corresponding bit of INTR_STATE clears the latched value, but if the event itself is still active, the INTR_STATE register will return to true.
rules.condition: Software writes 1 to the INTR_STATE bit
rules.statement: A write of 1 to an INTR_STATE bit clears the latched value, but INTR_STATE returns to true if the event is still active.

rules.quote: The hardware does not have the ability to clear the latched interrupt state, only software does.
rules.statement: Hardware must not clear the latched interrupt state; only software can clear it.

rules.quote: Each peripheral can send zero or more alerts, where each is a distinguishable security threat.
rules.statement: Each peripheral can send zero or more alerts, each a distinguishable security threat.

rules.quote: Each alert originates in some internal event, and must be specially handled within the peripheral, and then within the alert handler module.
rules.statement: Each alert originates in an internal event and must be specially handled within the peripheral and then within the alert handler module.

rules.quote: Alerts of comportable IPs in the system must be in either of the following two categories: *Recoverable*, one-time triggered alerts. This category is for regular alerts that are due to recoverable error conditions. The alert sender transmits one single alert event when the corresponding error condition is asserted.
rules.statement: A recoverable alert must be one-time triggered: the alert sender transmits a single alert event when the error condition is asserted.

rules.quote: Alerts of comportable IPs in the system must be in either of the following two categories: *Fatal* alerts that are continuously triggered until reset. This category is for highly critical alerts that are due to terminal error conditions. The alert sender continuously transmits alert events until the system is reset.
rules.statement: A fatal alert must be continuously transmitted by the alert sender until the system is reset.

rules.quote: It is recommended that fatal alerts also trigger local security countermeasures, if they exist.
rules.condition: Fatal alert and local countermeasures exist
rules.statement: Fatal alerts should also trigger local security countermeasures.

rules.quote: The table below lists a few common error conditions and the recommended alert type for each of those errors. (x): optional
rules.statement: Error conditions should use the recommended alert type listed in the table; the regular IRQ column entries marked (x) are optional.

rules.quote: The column "Regular IRQ" indicates whether the corresponding error condition should also send out a regular IRQ. A peripheral may optionally send out an IRQ for any alert event, depending on whether this is needed by the programming model to make forward progress.
rules.statement: A peripheral may optionally send a regular IRQ for any alert event, if needed by the programming model.

rules.quote: In terms of naming convention, alerts shall be given a meaningful name that is indicative of its cause.
rules.statement: Alerts shall be given a meaningful name indicative of their cause.

rules.quote: Recoverable alerts must be prefixed with recov_*, whereas fatal alerts must be prefixed with fatal_*.
rules.statement: Recoverable alerts must be prefixed with recov_ and fatal alerts must be prefixed with fatal_.

rules.quote: In such cases, it is permissible to default the alert names to just recov and/or fatal. Note that this implies that the peripheral does not expose more than one alert for that type.
rules.condition: Many diverse sources bundled into one alert event
rules.statement: Alert names may default to just recov and/or fatal, implying no more than one alert of that type is exposed.

rules.quote: For every peripheral, by default, one register named ALERT_TEST is automatically created. ALERT_TEST is a write-only (wo) register that allows software to test the reporting of alerts in the alert handler.
rules.statement: Every peripheral has a write-only (wo) ALERT_TEST register for software to test alert reporting in the alert handler.

rules.quote: Every alert of a peripheral has one field bit inside the ALERT_TEST register, and each field bit is meant to be connected to the test input of the corresponding prim_alert_sender (see next subsection).
rules.statement: Every alert has one field bit in ALERT_TEST, connected to the test input of the corresponding prim_alert_sender.

rules.quote: Internal events are sent active-high to a piece of IP within the peripheral called the prim_alert_sender.
rules.statement: Internal events are sent active-high to the prim_alert_sender within the peripheral.

rules.quote: One prim_alert_sender must be instantiated per distinct alert event, and the IsFatal parameter of the alert sender must be set to 1 for fatal alerts (this causes the alert sender to latch the alert until the next system reset).
rules.statement: One prim_alert_sender must be instantiated per distinct alert event, with IsFatal set to 1 for fatal alerts so the alert is latched until reset.

rules.quote: It is up to the peripheral maintainer to determine what are distinct alert events; multiple ones can be bundled depending upon the distinction required within the module (i.e. high priority threat vs. low level threat).
rules.statement: The peripheral maintainer determines distinct alert events; multiple sources can be bundled depending on the required distinction.

rules.quote: As a general guideline, it is recommended that each peripheral bundles alert sources into one or two distinct alerts, for example one fatal and one recoverable alert.
rules.statement: Each peripheral should bundle alert sources into one or two distinct alerts, for example one fatal and one recoverable.

rules.quote: It is recommended that comportable IPs with multiple bundled alerts expose a cause register for disambiguation, which is useful for debugging and crash dumps.
rules.condition: Comportable IP with multiple bundled alerts
rules.statement: The IP should expose a cause register for disambiguation.

rules.quote: Cause registers for recoverable alerts must either be clearable by SW, or the HW must provide an automatic mechanism to clear them (e.g., upon starting a new transaction initiated by SW).
rules.statement: Cause registers for recoverable alerts must be clearable by SW or automatically cleared by HW.

rules.quote: Cause registers for fatal alerts must not be clearable in any way and must hence be read-only.
rules.statement: Cause registers for fatal alerts must not be clearable in any way and must be read-only.

rules.quote: The prim_alert_sender converts the event into a differentially encoded signal pair to be routed to the hardware alert handler, as dictated by the details in the alert handler specification.
rules.statement: The prim_alert_sender converts the event into a differentially encoded signal pair routed to the hardware alert handler.

rules.quote: The alert handler module is automatically generated to have enough alert ports to represent each alert declared in the different included peripheral IP configuration files.
rules.statement: The alert handler is generated with enough alert ports for each alert declared in the included peripheral configuration files.

Interrupts are critical and common enough to standardize across the project.
(An alternate standard is the use of edge-triggered interrupts, which are not described here, but may be supported in a future release.)
Interrupts sent to the processor are aggregated by a platform level interrupt controller (PLIC).
Within that logic there may be another level of control for enabling, prioritizing, and enumeration.
Specification of this control is defined in the rv_plic documentation of the corresponding toplevel design.
The .hjson configuration file for a peripheral specifies interrupts with the field 'interrupt_list'.

All peripheral interrupts have equal severity, but may be classified into a hierarchy at a higher level, such as at a platform interrupt controller.
The determination of which input has interrupted the processor, sometimes referred to as "Disambiguation", is done primarily by querying the rv_plic claim/complete register (CC).
Interrupts are a mechanism for hardware to request attention from software, commonly as either a normal part of a system's operation or as a way to handle exceptional circumstances.
One way to design robust control flows and abstractions using interrupts is to model Interrupts + Interrupt Handlers as forming a handshaking interaction between hardware and software.
Hardware creates an interrupt request when a condition is true or an event occurs.
Software responds to this request, possibly performing some action to address the condition/event, then acknowledges the interrupt request as completed.

This request/acknowledge sequence is one way to mitigate the effects of non-determinism in a real system, such as race-conditions due to the inherent round-trip latency from signaling to handling, and the unknown latency of a core executing the handler for one of possibly many competing interrupt requests.
Event type: Whenever an instantaneous event occurs, trigger an interrupt request.
The names *Event* and *Status* are OpenTitan terminology.
Generic hardware prim_intr_hw is defined which generates interrupt requests for each type by using a parameter at the time of instantiation.
An instantaneous *Event* could be an error occurring, a counter value crossing a threshold, or a particular transition between two abstract states inside the peripheral.
For example, an event interrupt request implies that "the event happened at some point in the past (since we last acknowledged this interrupt)".
A status interrupt request means that "the condition is currently true".
Event type interrupts are latched indications of defined peripheral events that have occurred and have not yet been acknowledged by the processor.
For instance, the GPIO module might detect the rising or falling edge of one its inputs as an interrupt event.

Alerts are another critical and common implementation to standardize for all peripherals.
Unlike interrupts, there is no software component to alerts at the peripheral, though there is at the hardware alert handler.
See that specification for full details.
A general description of the handling of alerts at the hardware level is given here.
Alerts are sent as a bundled output from a peripheral to the hardware alert handler.
For example, a redundantly encoded FSM that is glitched into an invalid state is typically considered to be a fatal error condition.
In this case, a local countermeasure could be to move the FSM into a terminal error state in order to render the FSM inoperable until the next reset.

Note that while alerts may eventually lead to a system wide reset, this is not guaranteed since the alert response depends on the alert handler configuration.
The Hjson configuration file defined above specifies all that needs to be known about the alerts in the standard case.

For instance, an uncorrectable parity error in SRAM could be named fatal_parity_error.

In cases where many diverse alert sources are bundled into one alert event (see Alert Hardware Implementation), it may sometimes be difficult to assign the alert event a meaningful and descriptive name.
This helps to keep the total number of alerts (and their physical impact) low at the system level.
